_comment: the client's ACP manifest: everything here except the agent table and the personas, which are built from the ACP Registry and agent/config. Served at GET /api/v1/acp/manifest; the client fetches it every few hours, so editing this file and deploying changes the client without a release. Never put a key or secret in this file.
_installableComment: agents the client may install itself, into a folder of its own, when the user asks it to. An npx entry: the registry's exact package version, plus extraPackages, on runtimes.node. A binary entry: the registry's archives, each with the registry's sha256 or, where it gives none, the one pinned here for that exact url (sha256: {url: hash}; a new release is offered once its archives are pinned). Bump a pin here and deploy: clients offer the update.
_runtimesComment: runtimes the client installs for installable agents. Official archives only, each with the sha256 from that release's SHASUMS256.txt; bin is the programs' folder once the archive's top-level folder is removed.

claude-acp.signInText: open a terminal, run `claude` and sign in (type /login if it does not ask). An Anthropic API key, Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex set up for Claude Code also works.

gemini.signInText: Google's subscription sign-in for Gemini CLI has been retired (Google now offers Antigravity for that). Use Vertex AI, or set GEMINI_API_KEY in your shell profile (aistudio.google.com/apikey), then press Reconnect.

codex-acp.signInText: sign in with your ChatGPT account when Codex asks (or set OPENAI_API_KEY in your shell profile), then press Reconnect.

github-copilot-cli.signInText: sign in with your GitHub account when Copilot asks (it needs a GitHub Copilot plan), then press Reconnect.

antigravity-acp.signInText: sign in with your Google account (your Google AI subscription) when Antigravity asks, then press Reconnect.

cursor.signInText: open a terminal and run `cursor-agent login`, then press Reconnect.

auggie.signInText: open a terminal and run `auggie login`, then press Reconnect.

opencode.signInText: open a terminal and run `opencode auth login`, then press Reconnect.

goose.signInText: open a terminal and run `goose configure` to choose a provider and sign in, then press Reconnect.

qwen-code.signInText: open a terminal, run `qwen` and sign in when it asks, then press Reconnect.

discuss_model_with_seldon.howToRespond: You are Seldon, the expert System Dynamics discussant. Answer `request.prompt` following engineBrief, reasoning over the model and its loop dominance (loopDominance). Reply as text; do not edit the model.

discuss_model_across_runs.howToRespond: You are the plain-language discussant who compares runs. Following engineBrief, answer `request.prompt` without jargon, explaining what differs between the runs and why, using the loop dominance (loopDominance). Reply as text; do not edit the model.

generate_ltm_narrative.howToRespond: You are the Loops That Matter narrative engine. Following engineBrief, write the narrative of which feedback loops drive the model's behavior, when, and why, from loopDominance. Reply as text.

discuss_with_mentor.howToRespond: You are now the mentor. Following engineBrief, answer `request.prompt`: explain what you see in the model and its loop dominance (loopDominance), and ask the questions that help the user see what could be improved. Reply as text; do not edit the model.

model: Which model answers. Larger models are more capable on hard modeling problems, and slower, and use more of your account's usage.
model.default: The model your assistant uses when nothing is chosen (its own default, or your terminal configuration).
model.sonnet: Balanced: capable and quick. A good everyday choice for building and explaining models.
model.haiku: Fastest and lightest. Good for quick questions and small edits; less reliable on large models.
model.opus: Most capable. Best for complex models, analysis and multi-step builds; slower and uses more usage.
model.opus[1m]: Most capable, with a very long memory (1M tokens) for long sessions and large models. Uses more usage.

effort: How much the assistant thinks before it answers and acts. Higher is more thorough and slower, and uses more of your account's usage.
effort.default: Whatever your own configuration of the assistant says (e.g. effortLevel in Claude Code's settings).
effort.low: Quick answers with little deliberation. Fine for simple questions and small changes.
effort.medium: Balanced. Recommended for most modeling work.
effort.high: More careful reasoning for harder modeling questions and larger builds.
effort.xhigh: Very thorough. Noticeably slower; for difficult analysis.
effort.max: The most deliberation the model can do. Slowest, and the heaviest on usage.

mode: How much the assistant may do on its own before asking you. The application's own tools are always allowed.
mode.default: Asks before it edits files or runs commands.
mode.acceptEdits: Edits files in its working folder without asking; still asks before running commands.
mode.plan: Plans only: reads and proposes, changes nothing until you approve its plan.
mode.auto: The assistant decides which of its actions are safe to run without asking.
mode.bypassPermissions: Runs every action, including commands and file changes anywhere, without asking. Use with care.
mode.yolo: Runs every action, including commands and file changes anywhere, without asking. Use with care.
mode.agent-full-access: Runs every action, including commands and file changes anywhere, without asking. Use with care.
mode.full-access: Runs every action, including commands and file changes anywhere, without asking. Use with care.
mode.autopilot: Runs every action, including commands and file changes anywhere, without asking. Use with care.

fast: Faster responses from the same model, at a higher cost in usage.
fast.on: Faster responses; uses more of your account's usage.
